1.title: THE CONTENT FRAMEWORK — DELIVERABLES, ARTIFACTS & BUILDING BLOCKS
1.text: Welcome to Module 9. We've seen where architecture assets are stored and how they're classified. Now we look at what those assets actually are, and how they're structured — through the Content Framework. This module nails down three terms that thread through the entire exam: deliverables, artifacts, and building blocks. We'll also sharpen the ABB-versus-SBB distinction one more time, because it's tested everywhere. These are core vocabulary, so let's make them precise and permanent.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's the plan. You'll be able to explain the Content Framework and why it exists. You'll define and clearly distinguish deliverables, artifacts, and building blocks. You'll classify any artifact as a catalog, a matrix, or a diagram. You'll distinguish ABBs from SBBs in real depth. And you'll describe the Enterprise Metamodel and how building blocks get specified as the ADM progresses. The two highest-yield ideas to lock in are the deliverable-artifact-building-block trio, and the ABB-versus-SBB distinction. Both pay off across the entire exam, not just in this module.

1.title: What Is the Content Framework?
1.text: Let's define the Content Framework. It's a structural model for architectural content that allows your major work products to be consistently defined, structured, and presented. Crucially, it's organized in line with the ADM phases — so the structure of your content mirrors the method that produces it. And it defines the categorization for all the building blocks and artifacts that end up in the Architecture Repository. So in one sentence: the Content Framework gives a consistent structure to everything the ADM produces, which is exactly what you need when many architects are working across many projects over time.

1.title: Why the Content Framework Matters
1.text: Why bother with it? The standard gives several reasons. It provides a detailed model of architectural work products, so people know what good output looks like. It drives consistency in the outputs you create following the ADM. It acts as a comprehensive checklist of the architecture output you could produce — which reduces the risk of gaps in your final deliverable set. And it helps an enterprise mandate standard architecture concepts, terms, and deliverables. If you boil all of that down, two benefits stand out: consistency, and completeness as a checklist. Those two phrases will serve you well if the exam asks why the Content Framework exists.

1.title: The 3 Categories of Work Product
1.text: Here's the heart of the module — the three categories of work product. A deliverable is a contractually specified work product that's formally reviewed and signed off by stakeholders. An artifact is a work product that describes a single aspect of the architecture — and it takes the form of a catalog, a matrix, or a diagram. And a building block is a potentially reusable component that you combine with others to deliver architectures and solutions. The relationships matter, and the diagram shows them: a deliverable contains artifacts, and artifacts are views of building blocks. Memorize that chain — deliverable contains artifacts, artifacts are views of building blocks — because it's the backbone of this whole topic.

1.title: Deliverables in Depth
1.text: Let's go deeper on deliverables. The defining characteristic is that a deliverable is contractually specified, and it's formally reviewed, approved, and signed off by the stakeholders. It represents the output of projects. And when a deliverable is in documentation form, it's typically archived at the end of the project, or transitioned into the Architecture Repository — perhaps as a reference model, a standard, or a snapshot of the architecture landscape at a point in time. So if you remember one thing about deliverables, make it the sign-off: a deliverable is the formally agreed, contractual output. That's what separates it from a mere artifact.

1.title: Examples of TOGAF Deliverables
1.text: Let's ground that with examples, because you've actually met most of TOGAF's deliverables already. The Architecture Vision, the Statement of Architecture Work, and the Request for Architecture Work are all deliverables. So are the Architecture Definition Document and the Architecture Requirements Specification. So are the Architecture Roadmap and the Implementation and Migration Plan. And so are the Architecture Contract, and indeed the Architecture and Solution Building Blocks themselves. The exam-relevant skill is to connect each deliverable to the phase that produces it — which is exactly the phase-by-phase knowledge you built up in Modules 2 through 7. This module just gives them their category name: deliverables.

1.title: Artifacts in Depth
1.text: Now artifacts in depth. An artifact describes one specific aspect of the architecture — a single, focused view. Artifacts are classified as catalogs, matrices, or diagrams, and collectively they form the content of the Architecture Repository. Here's a subtlety the exam likes: an artifact may or may not be a deliverable — it depends on the contractual specification. If your contract says a particular diagram must be formally delivered and signed off, then that artifact is also a deliverable; if not, it's just an artifact. So the relationship is: a deliverable is a whole signed-off package that may contain many artifacts, while an artifact is a single aspect that's sometimes, but not always, a deliverable in its own right.

1.title: The 3 Types of Artifact
1.text: Let's nail the three artifact types, because this is tested again and again. A catalog is a list of things — for example, a requirements catalog or an application portfolio catalog. A matrix shows relationships between things — for example, an application interaction matrix, or a data-to-function matrix that maps which data each function uses. And a diagram is a picture of things — for example, a value chain diagram or an application communication diagram. The memory hook is simple and worth repeating until it's automatic: catalog equals list, matrix equals relationships, diagram equals picture. Given any artifact name, you should be able to slot it into one of those three.

1.title: Building Blocks in Depth
1.text: On to building blocks. A building block is a potentially reusable component of business, IT, or architectural capability. A key property is that it's defined at varying levels of detail depending on how far the ADM has progressed — early on, a building block might be just a name or an outline description; later, it might be decomposed into supporting building blocks and accompanied by a full specification. Building blocks relate either to architectures, in which case they're ABBs, or to solutions, in which case they're SBBs. The exam-relevant idea here is that building blocks become more detailed as architecture development matures — they're not fully specified from day one.

1.title: Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs)
1.text: Let's separate the two kinds of building block, starting with Architecture Building Blocks. An ABB describes a required capability, and it shapes the specification of the Solution Building Blocks that will eventually realize it. ABBs capture the "what" at the architecture level — they're deliberately independent of any particular implementation. They're typically defined across Phases A through D, as you develop the architecture. The standard's examples are things like a customer services capability, or a network. Both are abstract capabilities, not products. So lock it in: an ABB is the required capability, the "what," and it shapes the SBBs that come later.

1.title: Solution Building Blocks (SBBs)
1.text: Now Solution Building Blocks. An SBB is a physical or supplier-specific component that realizes a required capability. Where the ABB was the "what," the SBB is the "with what" — the actual implementation choice. SBBs typically appear from Phase E onward, in Opportunities and Solutions, when you start selecting real solutions to fill the gaps. Continuing the earlier examples: a specific vendor's CRM product would be an SBB realizing the abstract "customer services" ABB. So the clean statement is: an SBB is the implementation, the "with what," and it realizes an ABB. ABB first, SBB second; capability first, product second.

1.title: ABB vs SBB — Side by Side
1.text: Let's put ABBs and SBBs side by side, because the contrast is worth real marks. An ABB describes required capability; an SBB describes the implementation. The ABB answers "what"; the SBB answers "with what." The ABB is implementation-independent; the SBB is supplier or product specific. The ABB lives in the Architecture Continuum; the SBB lives in the Solutions Continuum. And ABBs cluster in Phases A through D, while SBBs appear from Phase E onward. The relationship has a clear, one-way direction: ABBs shape SBBs, and SBBs realize ABBs. Never the reverse. If you can reproduce this table, the exam's ABB-SBB questions become easy points.

1.title: The Building Block Specification Process
1.text: Let's see how building blocks get specified over time, because this is a process, not a one-shot definition. In the Vision and early phases, building blocks are identified by name or outline — mostly ABBs. Through Phases B, C, and D, those ABBs are elaborated with proper specifications. And in Phases E and F, SBBs are selected to realize the ABBs. So a building block's specification evolves alongside the architecture itself, getting steadily more concrete. The exam point is to resist the assumption that building blocks are fully nailed down at the start — in TOGAF, they're refined progressively as the ADM proceeds. Abstraction first, concreteness later.

1.title: Characteristics of a Good Building Block
1.text: What makes a building block a good one? Several characteristics. It should be loosely coupled and highly cohesive — meaning it does one well-defined thing, with minimal dependencies on other blocks. It should be reusable across multiple architectures and solutions, which is the whole point. It should have published interfaces, so other components can access its functionality in a defined way. And it should be able to interoperate with other building blocks, potentially including third-party ones. If you remember three adjectives, make them cohesive, loosely coupled, and reusable — those capture the essence of good building-block design and are the most likely to be tested.

1.title: How They Fit Together — A Worked Example
1.text: Let's tie the three categories together with the standard's own worked example. An Architecture Definition Document is a deliverable — it's a formally signed-off package. Inside it sit many artifacts. One of those artifacts might be a process flow diagram, which is a view of building blocks — for instance, the "call handling process," which is itself a building block. And that same diagram might also describe other building blocks, such as the actors involved in the process, like a Customer Services Representative. So you can see the whole chain in action: a deliverable contains artifacts, and those artifacts are views of building blocks. Internalize that chain and the relationships will never confuse you.

1.title: The Content Framework by ADM Phase
1.text: Let's see how the Content Framework is actually organized — and reassuringly, it mirrors the ADM. The work products fall into categories: Principles, Vision, Motivation, and Requirements, which align with the Preliminary Phase, Phase A, and Requirements Management; Business Architecture, aligned with Phase B; Information Systems Architecture, aligned with Phase C and its Data and Application halves; Technology Architecture, aligned with Phase D; Realization and Transformation, aligned with Phases E and F; and Architecture Change Management, aligned with Phase H. So you don't need to memorize a separate structure — the Content Framework follows the ADM phases you already know. That alignment is itself the thing to remember.

1.title: The Enterprise Metamodel
1.text: Now the Enterprise Metamodel, which is how TOGAF 10 frames the underlying "schema" for your models. The Enterprise Metamodel defines the types of entity that appear in the models describing the enterprise, together with the relationships between those entities. The standard gives a nice example: one entity type might be Role, and your business architecture would then contain instances of Role like Teller, Pilot, Manager, or Customer. Why do this? It provides consistency, completeness, and traceability across all your models. So think of the Enterprise Metamodel as the schema — the definition of entity types and relationships — that everything else in your architecture is an instance of.

1.title: The Core Enterprise Metamodel
1.text: TOGAF doesn't leave you to invent the metamodel from nothing. The TOGAF Library includes a Foundation-level Core Enterprise Metamodel, which shows the entity types and relationships likely to be needed when modeling most enterprises. It's deliberately a starting point — organizations are expected to tailor it into their own Organization-Specific Metamodel, adding or trimming entities as their context demands. So, consistent with TOGAF's whole philosophy, you get a Core metamodel as a head start, and you tailor it. Don't picture using it verbatim; picture adapting it. Core provided, tailoring expected — that's the pattern, exactly as with the rest of the framework.

1.title: Metamodel — Notation Independence
1.text: An important point that the exam sometimes probes: TOGAF does not constrain your choice of artifacts or your modeling notation. You're free to use ArchiMate, BPMN, UML, entity-relationship diagrams, flowcharts, or any other notation that can express the ideas. The metamodel defines what to model — the entities and relationships; the notation is simply how you choose to draw it. So if a question claims TOGAF mandates ArchiMate or UML, that's false. TOGAF is notation-agnostic, and ArchiMate in particular is complementary to TOGAF, designed to work alongside it, but never required by it. What versus how, one more time.

1.title: Deliverable vs Artifact vs Building Block — Lock It In
1.text: Let's lock in the three-way distinction with one consolidated table. A deliverable is a signed-off output; an artifact is one aspect; a building block is a reusable component. Is it contractual? A deliverable, yes; an artifact, maybe; a building block, no. In granularity, a deliverable is a whole package, an artifact is a single view, and a building block is a unit of capability or implementation. And for examples: an Architecture Definition Document is a deliverable, an application communication diagram is an artifact, and a network is an ABB while a CRM product is an SBB. This three-way distinction is one of the most-tested ideas in the entire exam — give it the attention it deserves.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: Let's clear the traps. One: "an artifact is always a deliverable" — no, it may or may not be, depending on the contract. Two: "an SBB describes the required capability" — no, that's the ABB; the SBB is the implementation. Three: "a matrix is a list" — no, a catalog is a list; a matrix shows relationships. Four: "TOGAF mandates ArchiMate or UML" — no, TOGAF is notation-agnostic. And five: "building blocks are fully specified up front" — no, they're refined progressively through the ADM. The two trap-rich areas to guard most carefully are the catalog-matrix-diagram classification and the ABB-versus-SBB distinction.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Your cheat-sheet. Three work-product categories — deliverable, artifact, building block. Three artifact types — catalog, matrix, diagram. Two building block types — ABB and SBB. A deliverable's defining trait is being signed off, or contractual. An ABB is the required capability, the "what"; an SBB is the implementation, the "with what." The Content Framework is structured by the ADM phases. And the metamodel provides entity types and relationships, delivering consistency, completeness, and traceability. Capture this — it's the densest set of definitions in the module.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's recap. The Content Framework gives a consistent structure to ADM outputs and doubles as a completeness checklist. There are three work-product categories: deliverables, which are signed off; artifacts, which are catalogs, matrices, or diagrams; and building blocks, which are reusable. ABBs define required capability while SBBs are the implementations, and ABBs shape SBBs. The Enterprise Metamodel defines entity types and relationships, and TOGAF is notation-agnostic about how you draw them. And the chain that ties it together: a deliverable contains artifacts, which are views of building blocks. Core vocabulary, now firmly in place.

1.title: Bridge to Module 10
1.text: Where does this lead? Notice that artifacts don't appear from nowhere — they're built from viewpoints that address specific stakeholder concerns. And in large enterprises, architectures have to be partitioned to keep the complexity manageable. Both of those ideas — partitioning, and views and viewpoints — are the subject of Module 10. The connecting thread to carry forward is this: views and viewpoints are precisely what turn abstract building blocks into stakeholder-relevant artifacts. So having defined the work products here, we'll next see how they're shaped to speak to particular stakeholders.

1.title: Quick Self-Check
1.text: A quick self-check. From memory: can you define deliverable, artifact, and building block in one line each? Can you give the three artifact types with an example of each? Can you state the direction of the ABB-to-SBB relationship — which shapes which? And can you say what the Enterprise Metamodel defines? If the catalog-matrix-diagram classification feels even slightly shaky, go back and re-watch slide nine — it's a guaranteed source of exam marks, and it's easy to lock in with a little repetition.

1.title: Memory Hook
1.text: Here's a tidy memory hook — just think D-A-B. D is for Deliverable: Done and signed, contractual. A is for Artifact: A single aspect, in the form of a catalog, matrix, or diagram. And B is for Building block: Build once, reuse many — where the ABB is the "what" and the SBB is the "with what." D-A-B: a signed package, a single aspect, a reusable component. Three letters that carry the entire structure of this module. Whenever a question throws these terms at you, run through D-A-B in your head and the answer will usually fall right out.

1.title: Why This Module Is High-Value
1.text: Let me stress why this module punches above its weight. These definitions don't stay politely inside Module 9 — they appear across the whole exam. A huge number of phase questions secretly hinge on "is this a deliverable or an artifact?" or "is this an ABB or an SBB?" So the effort you put into mastering these distinctions pays dividends on questions that, on the surface, look like they're about something else entirely. Treat the deliverable-artifact-building-block trio, and the ABB-SBB split, as foundational vocabulary — and over-learn them rather than just recognizing them. The return on that investment is exceptional.

1.title: One-Line Recap of the Supporting Concepts So Far
1.text: Let's take stock of the supporting concepts we've assembled. From Module 8: the Continuum classifies assets from generic to specific, and the Repository stores them in eight components. From this module: the Content Framework structures work products by ADM phase, and building blocks come in two kinds — the ABB, which is the "what," and the SBB, which is the "with what." A clean way to hold the trio: the Continuum classifies, the Repository stores, and the Content Framework structures. Three complementary lenses on the same body of architecture work. Next, we add views, viewpoints, and partitioning.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question 1. What distinguishes a deliverable from an artifact in the TOGAF Content Framework? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. A deliverable is contractually specified and formally signed off; an artifact describes a single aspect of the architecture and may or may not be a deliverable A deliverable is contractually specified, formally reviewed, and signed off. An artifact describes a single aspect of the architecture (a catalog, matrix, or diagram) and may or may not be a deliverable depending on the contract. A deliverable can contain many artifacts.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question 2. The TOGAF Content Framework classifies artifacts into three types. Which option lists them correctly? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. Catalogs, matrices, and diagrams Artifacts are classified as catalogs (lists of things), matrices (relationships between things), and diagrams (pictures of things). The other options mix in unrelated concepts.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question 3. Which statement correctly describes the relationship between ABBs and SBBs? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. ABBs describe required capability and shape the specification of SBBs, which are the implementations Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs) describe the required capability — the "what" — and shape the specification of Solution Building Blocks (SBBs), which are the physical/supplier-specific implementations — the "with what."

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question 4. What does the Enterprise Metamodel define? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. The types of entity that appear in architecture models and the relationships between them The Enterprise Metamodel defines the types of entity to appear in the models that describe the enterprise, together with the relationships between them. It supports consistency, completeness, and traceability, and TOGAF provides a tailorable Core Enterprise Metamodel.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question 5. Which statement about modeling notation in TOGAF is correct? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is C. TOGAF is notation-agnostic; ArchiMate, BPMN, UML, ER diagrams, and others may all be used TOGAF does not constrain the choice of modeling notation. It is notation-agnostic — you may use ArchiMate, BPMN, UML, entity-relationship diagrams, flowcharts, or any other suitable notation. ArchiMate is complementary to TOGAF, not mandated by it.
